On his return to Frankfort, he married a cousin of the tribe of Judah, and boldly set up a banking concern in a small way, the nucleus of the great house which now fills all Europe with its tame. By dint of probity, activity, and native aptitude for money making, the father of the present firm gamed more and more ground in the public confidence ; his credit extended and his clients increased. In 1801 Ins former illustrious numismatic patron, the Landgrave of Hesse, appointed Mr. Rothschild agent to his court. This was the first princely connexion of the concern, although they have since had dealings with, and in, sovereigns to pretty considerable amount, as the New York bard says. It was in this quality that Rothschild rendered very important services to the successor of the above named prince, especially when, in 1800, the latter, obliged to retire from his hereditary states at the approach of the French army could only carry off with him a comparatively inconsiderable sum in gold to which his whole fortune was then reduced. By his presence of mind, address, and ability, Mr. Rothschild contrived to save from the grasp of the loe the greatest part of the þÿLandgrave s property, but not without a few hair- þÿ þÿbreadth-scapes from the lynx-eyes, and drumhead justice of the Gallic intruders. Tim property so preserved from the plundering heroes, was conscientiously administered by Rothschild for Ins patron the prince. About this period the financial business of

the house of Rothschild began to assume importance, in consequence of its first loan, of ten millions of florins, to the court of Denmark. In 1812, Mayer Anselmo Rothschild, the father, was attacked by a mortal illness. Aware of his approaching end, he had his ten children called to his bed-side, gave them his dying benediction, and made them promise never to change their religion, and always to remain united amongst tilt ruse Ives on Change. These promises have been religiously kept, and amply has the fable of the bundle of sticks been verified by the live brothers. Whenever they are about to undertake an affair of importance, all tin; united brethren invoke the memory of their father, which is venerated by them in a manner highly honourable to their filial feelings. Their great political operations commenced in 1813, and up to the present time it is computed their house has negotiated in loans, subsidies, tec upwards of 1 GO, 000 millions sterling, principally for the different monarchs of Europe ; their profits have, of course,, been immense. Their long and uninterrupted success was owing to unanimity, and community of interests. Every proposition is decided by mutual deliberation. Each operation, major of or minor importance, is conducted upon a concerted and common plan ; and all their individual and combined energies arc employed to command success. Although for several years, they have resided at a distance from each other, that circumstance has by no means caused a distance, or

discord amongst them ; on the contrary, it has proved a great advantage, in contributing towards the prosperity of their immense undertakings, by thus making them au courant of the state ol the principal money-market of Europe, through a continual exchange of couriers, which generally precede the government messengers ; in this manner, each of the five brothers, from the point where he is placed, possesses a great facility for preparing and

In consequence of the new arrangement with the English Packets, we had the pleasure on Monday last the 16th instant, at 2 þÿo clock, p. m. to see the English Government Steamfcr the FLAMER, commanded by Lieutenant GRIFFIN, arrive in our Harbour, with the Mails from Jamaica, after a passage of 4 days and 21 hours. She brought Jamaica papers to the l'th instant, according to which all was quiet in that Island. It is evident, that tins easy and convenient wav of communication, must prove in the highest degree beneficial to the West India Interests, and that the different Islands have, in fact, been brought just as much nearer to each other, as the time is shorter, which it now takes and took formerly to go from one Colony to another. As yet, it seems that the Steamers have only orders to touch at Barbados, Jamaica and this Island, but it is expected, that they will hereafter have time enough likewise to run for one or more of the Windward Islands on their way back to Barbados. The rate of charges for passage in the Cabin is fixed as follows: from St Thomas to Barbados $25, or Five Pounds Sterling : from Barbados to Jamaica $50, or Ten Pounds Sterling: and from Jamaica to St. Thomas $50. As we have not had a Steamboat here in this Port for 8 or ft years, the Flamer was visited by a great number of the Inhabitants of the Town, who were most politely received I be agreed upon hereafter between their said and permitted to go over the Ship, which was j Majesties.
foi uid to be commodious and of large dimensions. She has an Engine of 120 horse pow- j er. She sailed the same day at 5 p. m.. and in 10 or 12 days we can expect another Steamer, the Spitfire.

The Wolf Rock, about seven miles to the S. VV. of the þÿLand E s nd, called a half-tide rock that is, appearing above water at half- þÿ ebb, would be a much more dangerous rock had not Providence so ordered it that, particularly in stormy weather, it makes a roaring noise so loud as to be heard a sufficient distance to warn the mariner of danger in the night-time or in thick weather. The rock is perpendicular, and no other rocks have been discovered of a dangerous nature near it, so that, a ship may pass on either side, at a few yards distance, in perfect safety. Should a ship be carried towards it in calm weather by the tide, although it may appear that inevitable destruction must be the consequence, yet near the rock there is such a strong reflux of tide, that the ship will be driven in a circular direction round the rock, but never touch it. There has been even an instance known of a ship driving thrice round the rock in one tide, but never coming in contact. 'The captain of this ship informed the writer that he landed on the rock, and as he stood on it with a lead and line plummed 36 fathoms perpendicularly.

The Folly of a Belief in Fortune Telling, or Astrology. þÿ The belief in Judicial Astrology, which appears to be adapted only to the darkest ages, continued, notwithstanding the vast progress made in literature and science, to be cherished pretty generally among the uneducated, and even, in too many instances, amongst the learned, until late in the seventeeth century, if indeed it did not even survive that date. To show the toce folly of all pretensions to the art of predicting future events from the positions of the stars, and the equal folly of believing in such predictions, the following anecdote is offered to the attention of our readers: Towards the middle and latter end of the seventeeth century, there lived a celebrated mathematician and astronomer, named James Ozanam, whose learned works are well known in every part of Europe. As an astronomer is continually gazing on the stars, and an astrologer professes to draw his predictions from them, the two were frequently confounded with each other. It happened that a nobleman of great rank, desirous of discovering the events of his future life, applied to Ozanam to draw his horoscope, and at the same time employed a neighbouring physician, who was also a professed and enthusiastic astrologer, to execute the same task. The physician complied; drew the horoscope, and of course pocketed his reward. As for Ozanam, he in vain represented to the nobleman, that he was no astrologer, þÿ that he did not believe in the

existence of such an art ; the nobleman persisted, and as he was a man whose positive commands were not to be refused, Ozanam, at length, threw together, at random, a parcel of predictions all promising riches, power, happiness, and every other worldly blessings that a man could desire. About twenty years afterwards, the same nobleman called again on Ozanam, loading him with compliments, and assuring him that every one of his predictions had been verified, while those of the physician turned out totall y false. The event confirmed both parties in their previous opinions. The nobleman, to whom Ozanam did not dare confess the trick, departed more firmly persuaded than ever, that astrology, in the hands of a really learned and able professor, was a science as true as the mathematics; while Ozanam, with much better reason, was confirmed in his opinion, that astrology had no existence whatever, except in the heated imagination of a few enthusiasts, the cunning of knaves, and the gullibility of fools.

'I he ( Government General in making this publicly known lor the information and compliance of all concerned with the admonition that these Conventions ol His Majesty will most rigidly be enforced, thinks it proper especially to recommend attention to the (5th Article of the additional Clause of the Convention of the 22nd March 1833, which is of the following tenor: þÿ Any merchant vessel of either of the two Nations visited and detained in pursuance of the Convention of the 30th of November 183 1 , and of the provisions hereinbefore recited, shall, unless proof be given to the contrary, be held and taken of right to have engaged in the Slave trade, or to have been fitted out for the purposes of such tratliek, if any of the particulars hereinafter specified shall be found in her outfit or equipment, or on board of her videlicet : 1 Having her hatches fitted with open gratings, instead of being close hatches, as usual in merchant-vessels ; 2 Having more divisions or bulkheads in the hold, or on deck, than necessary for trading vessels ; 3$ Having on board spare planks, either actually fitted in that shape, or fit tor readily

laying a second or moveable deck, or slave deck : 4 Having on board shackles, bolts, or hand cutis ; 5 Having on board a supply of water, more than sufficient for the consumption of her crew, as a merchant vessel ; P> Having on board an unreasonable number ot water casks, or other vessels for holding water, unless the master shall produce a certificate from the Custom-House from the place at which he cleared outwards, stating that a sufficient security had been given by the owners of such vessel, that such casks, or other vessels, should only be used for the reception of palm oil, or be employed in any other lawful trade ; 7 ) Having on board a greater quantity of mess tubs, or kids, than requisite for the use of her crew, us merchant vessel ; 8$ Having on board two or more copper boilers, or even one evidently larger than requisite for the use of her crew, as a merchant vessel ; Having on board a quantity of rice or farinha, flour of the manioc of Brazil, or cassada, or maize, or Indian corn, beyond probable requisite provision for the use of her crew.

The following ate the interesting particulars of a late shipwreck, wherein the sufferings and privations of the survivor are almost without a parallel in the chequered detail of the danger to which seamen are þÿexpose!, On the 4th ot -September, the brig Friendship, Captain N. t. Carder, sailed from Miraunicha, New Brunswick, with a cargo of timber for Bideford. On the morning of the 18th, she sprung a leak ; and on the 22d (the unremitting efforts ot the crpw at the pumps proving unavailing to keep her free ), she was full of water. In this de plorable condition, without the possibility of getting below, and distant, by their calculation, 347 league fro the coast of Ireland, they kept the vessel before the wind, Under easy sail, in the forlorn hope ef being able to make the land : but unhappily, on the 28th (when, by supposition, they were about 70 leagues from Cape Clear), a sudden squall coming on, she broached to, and overset.

By this melancholy disaster, two poor rumen were washed overboard and drowned, and the whole of the provisions and water they bed collected on deck, with both boats, and every moveable article were swept away. The rest of the crew, consisting of the captain, mate, three men, and four boys, with difficulty supported themselves on the side of the ship; when after remaining in this awful situation about 40 minutes, having in the mean time Carried away her foremast, bowsprit, and main- topmast, she righted. /Vom the conditien the vessel was in, however, sb« had gradually settled abaft, and from midships forward was the only part of the deck left above water, upon which the miserable survivors could obtain an insecure footing, every succeeding wave threatening to hurl them into the dreadful abyss j For six tedious days and nights did these devoted sufferers remain in this wretched and hopeless slate, without a morsel of bread to sustain the cravings of ji e tin e! all of them very thinly cloaihed, several without shoes, stockings or hats, end the few garments they wore constantly wet, owing to the rain fell, and the ea that broke over them. From the former, however, they fortunately derived some sustenance; for during rain, they suspended a bedquilt in the remnant of the rigging, and when completely saturated, by --carefully squeezing it, they obtained three pints of water at each trial ; with and a small quantity of rum, the only tliiw, with salt water, that Capt. State and Congressional Elections. The papers West and South of us have long been busy in conducting the usual electioneering warfare. Local policy seems to have had much todoin determining these affairs. The sharpest contests have been among "brethren oj' the same political principles." There are, however, some instances ol gain from federalism to republicanism. In Delaware and Maryland, while the state authorities continue federal, the representatives chosen to the next Congress, shew that a large majority of the people are republican.
